> [!note] Update 1 Notes (imported from Notion)
> Link:
> [https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/malleable-software/](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/malleable-software/)
> Type:
> Design essay / research concept / software philosophy
> Focus:
> How software could give users more control to adapt, modify, and reshape their digital tools.
> Main idea:
> Most modern software is designed as a finished product. Users can change a few settings, but they usually cannot meaningfully change how the software works. Malleable software proposes that users should be able to adapt software to their own needs with minimal effort.
> Software should not force users to adapt themselves to the tool. The tool should be able to adapt to the users.
> Different users have different needs, workflows, abilities, and preferences. A mass-produced application cannot anticipate every possible need.
> Why it is interesting:
> This is highly relevant to accessibility. Disabled users often have very specific and individual needs, but many products provide only general settings designed by the company.
> A more adaptable system could allow users to adjust:
> - Layout
> - Navigation
> - Text size
> - Information density
> - Input methods
> - Feedback types
> - Timing
> - Labels
> - Workflow
> - Output format
> Potential connection to my thesis:
> This gives me a way to think about accessibility beyond fixed features. Instead of designing one product for one "average" disabled user, I could explore how a digital tool allows users to make small adjustments according to their individual needs.
> Possible connection to AI:
> AI could help users customize software through natural language. For example, a user could say:
> - "Make this interface less crowded."
> - "Show me only the most important information."
> - "Give me more time to complete this task."
> - "Read this in simpler language."
> - "Use larger buttons."
> - "Turn these instructions into a checklist."
> However, AI should not make these decisions secretly. Users should be able to review, change, and undo the adaptations.
> Questions:
> - How much control do users need over their digital tools?
> - Which customizations are most valuable for disabled users?
> - Should customization be manual, automatic, or AI-assisted?
> - Can users understand what the system has changed?
> - How can a system remain simple while still being flexible?
> - Can different users share adaptations with each other?
> - How can users undo or correct an adaptation?
> - Is a highly flexible product always better?
> - Could too many choices create cognitive overload?
> Personal reflection:
> This essay helps me think about accessibility as adaptability. A product may not need to predict every user's needs in advance if it allows users to reshape the product themselves.

> Mechanic allows designers to turn their own design rules and decisions into reusable tools. Instead of manually producing every asset, the designer writes a function that generates images, videos, or other design outputs.
> What it does:
> - Turns design rules into functions
> - Generates assets in the browser
> - Creates custom project-specific design tools
> - Allows outputs such as SVG, PNG, and WEBM
> - Automates repetitive design work
> - Uses familiar web technologies
> - Provides a browser-based canvas for previewing designs
> Why it is interesting:
> Mechanic is not simply a design software like Figma or Photoshop. It allows designers to create a smaller, more personalised tool for a specific design problem.
> The interesting shift is:
> Instead of adapting my workflow to an existing software tool, I can create a tool that matches my workflow.
> What problem does it address:
> Many design tools are general-purpose and require designers to repeat similar processes manually. Mechanic allows designers to encode their decisions and automate repetitive production.
> Important design concept:
> Designers can become toolmakers.
> Potential connection to my thesis:
> This is relevant to my interest in software-based products and web tools. It suggests that a product does not always need to be a large platform or a complete application. It can be a small, focused tool designed around a specific user need or workflow.
> It may also be relevant to accessibility because different users may need different ways to work with software. Instead of forcing every user to use the same interface, a tool could allow users or communities to create customised workflows.
> Questions:
> - Could a future accessibility tool be customised by the users themselves?
> - Could users create their own interface, workflow, or output format?
> - How much customisation is useful before a tool becomes too complicated?
> - Can a tool adapt to different abilities without requiring users to code?
> - Could AI help users customise a tool using natural language?
> - What is the difference between personalisation and user-created tools?
> Limitations:
> Mechanic is mainly focused on designers and generated visual assets. It may require coding knowledge, so it is not immediately accessible to all users.
> This creates an interesting design question:
> How can a customisable tool be made accessible to people who are not programmers?
> Possible research direction:
> Designing a software tool that allows users to adapt a digital experience to their own needs without needing to write code.
> Personal reflection:
> Mechanic made me think about software not only as something I use, but also as something I can design and reshape according to a specific user group or workflow.
